You pass with a bounds-carrying check, correct on all five trees, and with O(n) and O(h) stated. A correct check with the extremes used as sentinel bounds is a partial pass. A check that compares each node only with its children is a fail, whatever it answers on your own test.

A binary search tree keeps one invariant: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is larger. That statement is about whole subtrees, not a node and its direct children, and reading it in order, left subtree then node then right subtree, produces ascending keys.
are this structure kept height-balanced through rotations, which is what most code should reach for rather than a hand-written tree.

The problem is holding a changing set of keys in sorted order, supporting search, insert and erase, without the O(n) shifts a sorted array needs on every insert, and without giving up range queries, such as the first key at or after a time stamp, that a hash map cannot answer.

The mechanism is a descent: at each node, one comparison says which subtree could hold the key, and the other subtree is never looked at again, so search, insert and erase each cost one step per level, the tree's height. Erase only looks complicated with two children, where the node's key is replaced by its in-order successor, the smallest key of its right subtree, and removing that successor falls back to the no-child or one-child case.

What happens when the tree is unbalanced is that its height stops being logarithmic. Keys inserted in already-sorted order, ordinary for time stamps or a replayed log, build a tree that is a linked list wearing a tree's type, height equal to the key count, so every operation degrades to O(n). A red-black tree such as
rebalances with rotations on insert and erase so the height stays O(log n) whatever order the keys arrive in, at the cost of one allocation per node and pointers a processor cannot prefetch.

The mistake that shows up under pressure is validating the invariant against only a node and its parent: a node can sit on the correct side of its own parent and still land in the wrong subtree of an ancestor further up, so a search that trusts the tree walks past a key that is there and returns false, with nothing crashing and no sanitizer firing. That is the interview question itself: checking whether a tree is a valid BST means carrying a shrinking range down from the root, not comparing each node with the one above it.

c.v: The same 4096 keys, the same code, two insertion orders. Sorted keys give a tree of height 4096, which is a linked list wearing a tree's type: every insert walks to the bottom, so building it costs n(n−1)/2 = 8,386,560 comparisons, and a lookup costs 2047.5 on average. Shuffled keys give height 28 and 13.6 comparisons per lookup, 150 times cheaper, and the perfectly balanced height for 4096 keys is 13. Sorted input is the ordinary case in a robot: time stamps, sequence numbers, sorted files and anything replayed from a log all arrive in order. This is the same 8,386,560 that the sorting topic measured for a textbook quicksort on sorted input, and for the same reason: an unbalanced split on every step.

In a binary search tree, the answer is the first node whose key stops both searches from going the same way. While both keys are below the node, both live in its left subtree, so the node is not the deepest common ancestor and the walk goes left; the mirror case goes right; anything else is the answer. In a tree with no ordering there is nothing to steer by, so the whole tree is searched and the answer is assembled on the way back up, which is a post-order:

c.v: The first tree is the one to remember. Every child is on the correct side of its own parent, so

Nothing crashes, no sanitizer fires, and the tree quietly loses a reading. Everything a binary search tree offers rests on the property holding for whole subtrees, so a validator that checks parents alone is checking a different, weaker thing. The same mistake appears as an insert that compares with the parent of the insertion point rather than walking from the root.

The second half is about equal keys, and the honest answer is that the invariant as stated has nothing to say about them: it puts smaller keys left and larger keys right, and a key equal to the node belongs to neither side. Strict rejects both trees, "equals on the left" accepts only the tree that puts the second 5 on the left, and "equals on the right" accepts only the other.
